newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Virginia a textbook case on capital punishment.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Virginia a textbook case on capital punishment.

text.p: This is the story of a man about to be executed, and death penalty experts agree it is about as good an example as there is of how capital punishment works in the United States.

It is the story of Coleman Wayne Gray, who is scheduled to be led into the execution chamber in a prison in southern Virginia on Feb. 26 and put to death by lethal injection. The tale is one of seemingly endless appeals to state and federal courts and of legal arguments that go beyond guilt or innocence to fundamental questions of fairness and justice.

Gray's final hopes to live lie with a U.S. Supreme Court that has already rejected his appeal once and with a bid for clemency to Virginia Gov. George Allen, who has stopped only one execution since 1994 while allowing 15 others to proceed.
Gray, now 39, was convicted in December 1985 of murdering shopkeeper Richard McClelland the previous May. The case has dragged on through state and federal courts for 11 years.

Death penalty advocates say killers like Gray benefit from endless appeals and delays. "Coleman Gray got a fair trial and has been before more courts than most people ever get an opportunity to address. He deserves the death penalty," C. Phillips Ferguson, the prosecutor at Gray's trial, said.

Gray's lawyer, Donald Lee, says his client was sentenced to die on the evidence of jailhouse snitches and an accomplice trying to save his own neck. He also charged that Gray was the victim of a "judicial ambush" staged by the prosecution. "He was sold out at trial, ambushed on sentencing and now faces a death penalty propped up by legal technicalities," Lee said.

On May 2, 1985, Gray and accomplice Melvin Tucker abducted McClelland as he was leaving his job as manager of Murphy's Mart in Portsmouth, Virginia. They took his car, drove him back to the store and forced him at gunpoint to unlock it.
After stealing $12,000, they drove McClelland to a remote road. Tucker said Gray then took McClelland behind the car and fired six shots into his head despite his pleas for his life.
GRAY INSISTS ACCOMPLICE WAS TRIGGERMAN
Gray admits he took part in the crime but insists Tucker was the killer. Under Virginia law only the triggerman can be sentenced to death.

Before the case came to trial in Virginia's Suffolk County the prosecutor made a deal with Tucker. In exchange for testifying against Gray, he was charged with the lesser offence of first degree murder and guaranteed a sentence of less than life imprisonment, making him eligible for parole soon.

A pool of 36 potential jurors showed up for the case. Of the eight black members, six were excused when they said they opposed the death penalty, the prosecution objected to one and the defence to the other, leaving Gray, who is black, to face an all-white jury.

He was defended by two court-appointed lawyers, neither of whom had ever previously defended a capital case, one where the defendant faces the death penalty. On the first day of the trial, one of his lawyers asked the court to order the prosecution to reveal what evidence it planned to introduce during the penalty phase if Gray was convicted.

Prosecutor Ferguson said he would bring forward witnesses who would testify that Gray had bragged about committing two other murders -- the December 1984 killings of Lisa Sorrell and her 3-year-old daughter Shanta. Gray's lawyer said: "If that comes in, we are going to want to know it in advance so we can be prepared on our argument. It's ... dynamite."
GORY EVIDENCE ON EARLIER KILLINGS

Ferguson said he would not bring up additional evidence relating to the Sorrell murders, in which neither Gray nor anyone else has ever been charged. But the prosecutor changed his mind, calling witnesses to testify about those killings and introducing gory photos and evidence from the 1984 case.

In an interview with Reuters, Ferguson defended his actions. "Under Virginia law, I was not required to inform them of anything. We were not even required to tell them that Tucker would testify about the Sorrell murders," he said.

Lisa Sorrell, who had been shot in the head six times with the same kind of gun that killed McClelland, was found in her partially burned car. Her daughter had been locked in the trunk and had apparently died of carbon monoxide inhalation.

Tucker testified that Gray had once boasted of "knocking off" Lisa Sorrell. But there was no motive or physical evidence linking him to the murders and the jury was not told that there was another strong suspect in the case. The defence, caught by surprise, never brought that up.

Gray's defence attorneys asked for all the Sorrell evidence to be excluded, but the judge ruled against them. And in his closing argument Ferguson said of Gray: "He's committed murder after murder, many in the same style. He's done it to Richard McClelland ... he did it to Lisa Sorrell and he even did it to Shanta Sorrell, the little daughter."

Under Virginia law, there are two criteria for the death penalty: the vileness of the crime and the future danger posed to society by the defendant. Linking Gray to the Sorrell murders vastly strengthened the prosecution's contention that Gray was a danger to society.
DEATH SENTENCE ON BOTH CRITERIA

The all-white jury deliberated for one hour and 10 minutes and sentenced Gray to death on both criteria. Gray appealed to the Virginia Supreme Court, which affirmed both the conviction and the death penalty in October 1987. More appeals followed and in January 1991 the state supreme court again ruled against him.

Gray then went to the Federal District Court in Richmond, which ruled in August 1994 that the prosecution had unfairly surprised Gray with the Sorrell evidence and had denied him the right to an effective defence. It vacated the death penalty.

The state took the case to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, which reinstated the death penalty in June 1995, ruling that the district court's decision was not backed by legal precedent. The case went back to Suffolk County where the circuit court set Gray's execution for Dec. 14, 1995. But Gray appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, which stayed the execution so it could review the case.

On June 20, 1996, the court by a 5-to-4 majority sided with the state of Virginia against Gray. Writing for the majority, Chief Justice William Rehnquist said the prosecution had not violated Gray's rights.

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, in a strong opinion for the dissenters, wrote: "Basic to due process in criminal proceedings is the right to a full, fair, potentially effective opportunity to defend against the state's charges. Petitioner Gray was not accorded that fundamental right at the penalty phase of his trial."

Ginsburg said Gray's lawyers were "reduced nearly to the role of spectators" at the crucial penalty phase and argued that the prosecution's behaviour had "fatally infected" its case for the death penalty.
